title: Debussy’s cathedral rises twice
work: La cathédrale engloutie, Préludes I, No. 10
question: How can the same piano sound like distant bells and a full cathedral organ?
intro: The bells come first: bare fifths sounding through Debussy’s mist. Then the piano becomes an organ, its C-major chords filling the keyboard before retreating to a quiet echo. Marcelle Meyer and Ivan Ilić recorded La cathédrale engloutie in Paris, fifty years apart.

recordings.label: Marcelle Meyer, 1956
recordings.note: Meyer, a pupil of Cortot and Viñes, brings a full piano tone and carefully judged pedalling to Debussy’s great chords.

recordings.label: Ivan Ilić, 2006
recordings.note: Ilić’s Paris recording gives the chords firm edges; flexible rhythms keep the phrases moving through their changes of pace.

passages.label: Opening fifths
passages.note: Bare Gs and Ds ring out quietly. Rising fifths leave wide spaces between the notes, like distant bells.

passages.label: First expansion
passages.note: Triplets start moving beneath the rising chords; the piano gathers strength as the cathedral emerges from the mist.

passages.label: Broad chordal span
passages.note: The organ-like tune stands in full C-major chords. Their top notes sing the melody above a deep bass.

passages.label: Quiet echo
passages.note: The great tune returns lower and pianissimo, over a gently moving bass. Debussy marks it as an echo of the earlier phrase.
